intro: A small boat, and an ocean that takes up the whole keyboard. In the third of Ravel’s Miroirs, a slow melody rides above arpeggios that grow from a ripple into great sweeping waves.

sections.label: A · A melody over rippling arpeggios
sections.mNote: F♯ minor, with slow upper notes and a restless left hand

sections.label: Link · Arpeggios sink into the bass
sections.mNote: The right hand falls silent above the descending left hand

sections.label: B · Chromatic runs and a long crescendo
sections.mNote: Both hands eventually sweep across the keyboard

sections.label: C · A melody marked très expressif
sections.mNote: The bass arpeggios slow beneath the singing line

sections.label: B′ · Sweeping runs under three flats
sections.mNote: Quiet tremolos alternate with fortissimo runs

sections.label: D · A high figure keeps circling
sections.mNote: Three sharps return; the left hand sings below repeated notes

sections.label: E · Tremolos in the lower keys
sections.mNote: The right-hand tremolo blends into a rolling bass

sections.label: A′ · The first ripple returns
sections.mNote: A brief reprise dwindles to a chord marked pppp

cues.title: Wrapped in pedal
cues.text: D’un rythme souple — très enveloppé de pédales: a supple rhythm, wrapped in pedal. The left hand keeps rising and falling beneath slow, tied notes in the right. Ravel writes two metres together, 6/8 and 2/4, so the boat rocks without a square, heavy beat.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), Une barque sur l’océan, opening page: paired 6/8 and 2/4 signatures, pedal instruction, arpeggios and tied upper notes. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs_DemetsEd.pdf, PDF p. 14.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: For the painter Paul Sordes
cues.text: Ravel dedicates the boat to Paul Sordes, a painter in his circle of friends, Les Apaches. Each of the five pieces in Miroirs carries an Apache’s name. Sordes gets the widest stretch of water.
cues.evidence: Arisa Tachi’s account of Miroirs identifies the five Apache dedications and Paul Sordes as a painter. https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329

cues.title: The first great wave
cues.text: Low bass notes start a long crescendo. The right hand runs through chromatic curves while the left strikes deep notes and rolled chords. Soon both hands sweep across the keyboard, their surges separated by quieter bars.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 17–19: one-beat sf bar, pp en dehors, crescendo and wide ff–fff runs. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs_DemetsEd.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A line begins to sing
cues.text: After the sweeping runs, a glissando leads into a phrase marked très expressif. The bass arpeggios move more slowly. The piano has room for a long singing line, with little surges still breaking through it.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 19: glissandi, the 2/4 continuation, très expressif and slower bass arpeggios.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A line from Julius Caesar
cues.text: Ravel explains the title Miroirs with a line from Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar: “The eye sees not itself / But by reflection, by some other things.” In 1928 he accepts the label “impressionist” only by analogy.
cues.evidence: The Shakespeare line (Julius Caesar, act 1, scene 2) is in Ravel’s Esquisse autobiographique, in English in Orenstein, A Ravel Reader (2003), p. 35, as quoted by Kyle Fyr, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 5: https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.4/mto.20.26.4.fyr.html. The remark on impressionism “by analogy” is in the same text, published in La Revue musicale, December 1938, in English in Ruti Abramovitch, “Maurice Ravel’s Miroirs for Piano” (Indiana University, 2012): https://scholarworks.iu.edu/dspace/bitstream/handle/2022/15206/Abramovitch_Ruti_2012.pdf

cues.title: Three flats, another wave
cues.text: Three flats replace the opening’s three sharps. High, quiet tremolos alternate with runs that plunge through both hands, marked fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 21–22: three-flat signature, pp tremolos and ff–fff runs. The returning sweep is also identified in Arisa Tachi’s formal account: https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The left hand sings
cues.text: Three sharps return. High in the right hand, a quick figure begins to circle, pianissimo and sans nuances — without shading. Below it the left hand has an expressive melody, with its own rises and falls.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 22–23: restored three-sharp signature, pp sans nuances in the right hand and p expressif in the left.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The circling figure grows
cues.text: The high repeated figure keeps turning while the notes beneath it thicken into chords. Ravel asks for a gradual increase. The hands spread out again, and the circling notes spill into another full-keyboard sweep.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 25–26: augmentez peu à peu, fuller chords, and ff–fff sweeps.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Aboard the yacht Aimée
cues.text: From 2 June to the end of July 1905 Ravel cruises the canals of France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany on the yacht Aimée, owned by Alfred and Misia Edwards. The painter Pierre Bonnard is among the guests. Miroirs is first played in January 1906.
cues.evidence: Manuel Cornejo’s Maurice Ravel chronology (1905): the trip of nearly two months aboard the yacht Aimée of Alfred and Misia Edwards, with Cipa and Ida Godebski, Pierre Bonnard and Pierre Laprade, on the canals of France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, from 2 June to about 29–31 July; première of Miroirs on 6 January 1906 (1906 entries): https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf

cues.title: A tremolo that melts
cues.text: The writing drops into the lower keys. A right-hand tremolo sits above rolling bass notes, and Ravel asks for it to be très fondu — thoroughly blended. The separate attacks dissolve into a low shimmer.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 27: both staves in the bass clef, repeated figures and le trémolo très fondu.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The boat comes back
cues.text: The opening ripple returns beneath the right hand’s tied notes. This time only a few phrases remain. Ravel lets the arpeggios climb and fall away, ending with a rolled chord marked pppp.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 30: brief return of the opening figure and final rolled pppp chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The right hand leaves space
transitions.from: A · A melody over rippling arpeggios
transitions.to: Link · Arpeggios sink into the bass
transitions.how: Ravel moves into 3/4, then 2/4, and lets the right-hand phrases dwindle to rests. The left hand continues alone, carrying its arpeggios deeper into the bass. The three-sharp signature stays in place while naturals loosen the harmony.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 16: changes of metre, right-hand rests and descending bass arpeggios.

transitions.title: One short bar launches the wave
transitions.from: Link · Arpeggios sink into the bass
transitions.to: B · Chromatic runs and a long crescendo
transitions.how: A one-beat bar marked sforzando interrupts the low arpeggios. In 3/4, the right hand starts chromatic runs, pp en dehors, while the left supplies rolled chords and deep bass notes. A long crescendo spreads the writing across both hands.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 16–17: 1/4 sf bar, 3/4, pp en dehors and the following crescendo.

transitions.title: A glissando clears the way
transitions.from: B · Chromatic runs and a long crescendo
transitions.to: C · A melody marked très expressif
transitions.how: The two-handed runs diminish. A right-hand glissando crosses above low bass octaves, then the piano settles into 2/4. The melody, marked très expressif, rests on slower arpeggios, with space between its long notes.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 19: diminuendo, glissando and très expressif continuation.

transitions.title: Three flats change the water
transitions.from: C · A melody marked très expressif
transitions.to: B′ · Sweeping runs under three flats
transitions.how: A double bar replaces three sharps with three flats. In 3/4, high pianissimo tremolos hover above a rising left-hand arpeggio. The next sweep breaks into common time at fortissimo, driving both hands down and back up the keyboard.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 21: new signature, 3/4 tremolo passage and common-time ff runs.

transitions.title: The high figure starts circling
transitions.from: B′ · Sweeping runs under three flats
transitions.to: D · A high figure keeps circling
transitions.how: A short très expressif phrase follows the sweep. Three sharps return, and the right hand climbs towards the top of the keyboard. Its quick notes settle into a repeating figure, pp sans nuances, above an expressive left-hand line.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 22–23: expressive link, restored signature and the contrasting instructions for the two hands.

transitions.title: The hands sink into the bass
transitions.from: D · A high figure keeps circling
transitions.to: E · Tremolos in the lower keys
transitions.how: The wide sweeps contract into repeated low figures. The right hand’s tremolo, now written in the bass clef, blends with the left hand’s rolling accompaniment. Ravel writes le trémolo très fondu and gradually reduces the piano’s force.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 26–27: descending sweeps, bass-clef tremolo and blending instruction.

transitions.title: Low chords release the first ripple
transitions.from: E · Tremolos in the lower keys
transitions.how: Low repeated chords diminish beneath short upper phrases. A rising run carries the hands back to the opening’s F♯-minor arpeggios, now pianissimo. The right hand restores its tied notes above them; only a brief reprise separates this return from the final pppp chord.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 30: low chords, rising link and return of the opening arpeggios.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
